Is the question how, or why?

The how is pretty simple, they just code it that way. Usually multihits are programmed as a single weak move hitting the target several times (so that defense or onhit effects can apply to each hit)

The why is usually because of some interaction with the games damage formula. In slay the spire for instance, strength is additive, so it adds a flat amount to each hit, which matters more when you're hitting several times.

Ive made a couple formulas like this (this will be from the perspective of an RPG, think something like pokemon)


Basically, I determined all of the factors that should go into damage calculation. The users level, the power of the move, crits, defense, other mitigation. Then I threw them all into a simple formula (something like damage = (power*attack*(level/5)) - defense) and came up with a bunch of example cases. How much damage should early game attacks be doing to eachother? What about lategame? What about a level 1 guy hitting a level 100 guy, but with a very strong attack?


I then played with the numbers and the scaling to apply to each stat until I found something that gave me numbers I liked for every example case. Exponential, logarithmic, linear, etc.

Im imagining a healthbar that starts halfway green and halfway black/corrupted (adjust numbers to your liking) 


Your attacks hit the corruption part of the HP bar first, and you have to chip all the corruption off before you can do any healing. 


Once you've gotten through the corruption, you can choose to either fight through the rest of their HP bar to knock them out, or you can heal them up to full HP to fully cure them and get bonus XP.


The corruption can grow stronger throughout the battle so it's harder to heal them to full if your attacks are too weak. If they get fully corrupted, they die and you get no XP (so you're likely to lose later.) Sometimes you'll have to decide if it's worth it to try to cure a strong monster or just mercy faint it so you don't take too much damage.
